title: Choosing an architecture pattern for multi-agent AI systems
excerpt: Three patterns, orchestrator-worker, blackboard, pipeline, solve coordination but each brings its own trade-offs and failure modes.
body:
A single well-tuned agent can look impressive in a short demo. Give it a clear goal, a handful of tools, and a generous system prompt, and it will answer a restaurant query or generate a code snippet in minutes. Adding a second agent flips the problem from “how does the agent reason?” to “how do the agents coordinate?” The coordination layer consumes most of the engineering effort once the system moves beyond a one-off demo.

The three patterns that keep reappearing when work is split across multiple agents are the orchestrator-worker model, the blackboard model, and the pipeline model. Each solves a different class of coordination problem and each brings its own failure modes that only surface after weeks of unattended operation. The source for this overview is the blog post [Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns](https://kadhar.dev/blog/multi-agent-systems-from-scratch).

## Orchestrator-worker pattern and its bottleneck

In the orchestrator-worker pattern a single manager agent receives the overall task, breaks it into subtasks, dispatches each subtask to a specialized worker, and finally aggregates the results. Workers never talk to each other; all communication passes through the orchestrator. The source diagram shows a concrete flow:

```
Task → Orchestrator
├─→ Worker A (research)
├─→ Worker B (code generation)
└─→ Worker C (validation)
↓ Orchestrator aggregates → Final answer
```

This layout works well when the decomposition is known upfront. If answering a question always requires a lookup, a generation step, and a validation step, the orchestrator can plan the three branches without needing to understand the details of each. Because the orchestrator’s prompt stays short, its behavior is more predictable and easier to evaluate.

A tradeoff appears as a bottleneck. Every piece of context, input, intermediate result, and final output must flow through the orchestrator. When the orchestrator mis-splits the work, all downstream workers inherit the mistake. Since aggregation also happens in the orchestrator, a slowdown or failure there stalls the entire pipeline. In production this single point of congestion often shows up as increased latency or dropped tasks once the system handles more concurrent requests than a demo ever did.

## Blackboard pattern for dynamic problem solving

The blackboard pattern drops the strict hierarchy. Instead of a central manager, all agents share a common state store, the “blackboard.” Each agent reads the current partial state, writes new hypotheses or evidence, and decides independently when to act. A lightweight scheduler may choose which agent runs next based on the blackboard contents, but no single agent owns the overall plan.

Visually, the pattern looks like this:

```
┌────────────────────────┐
│ Shared Blackboard       │
│ (partial state, facts, │
│ hypotheses)            │
└───────────┬────────────┘
   read/write │ read/write
   ┌─────────▼─────────┐
   │ Agent A  Agent B │
   │ (hypothesis) (evidence) │
   │ Agent C (critique) │
   └───────────────────┘
```

The blackboard shines when the solution path cannot be predicted in advance. Consider debugging a subtle production issue: one agent proposes a hypothesis, another gathers logs to support or refute it, and a third critiques the reasoning. Because each step depends on what has already been written to the blackboard, the workflow can adapt on the fly.

Complexity is the cost. Without a single plan holder, reproducing a failure requires reconstructing the entire sequence of reads and writes, a process similar to debugging a race condition. Tests become harder to write because the order of agent actions can vary with each run. The source notes that this flexibility makes blackboard systems “much harder to reason about and to test.”

## Pipeline pattern for fixed workflows

The pipeline pattern is the simplest of the three. It strings together a fixed sequence of specialized agents, each handing its output directly to the next. There is no delegation logic, no shared scratch space, just a straight chain:

```
Input → Retrieve Agent → Extract Agent → Validate Agent → Format Agent → Output
```

When the workflow is well-understood and repeatable, such as retrieving data, extracting relevant fields, validating them, and formatting the final response, the pipeline eliminates the need for a central planner or shared state. Each agent can be tuned in isolation, and the overall latency is the sum of the individual stages.

Because the sequence never changes, testing is straightforward: feed a known input and verify the final output. The source calls this the pattern to “default to whenever the workflow is well-understood and repeatable.” The downside is a lack of adaptability; if a new subtask is required, the pipeline must be rebuilt or an additional stage added, which can break existing contracts.

## The takeaway

Pick the orchestrator-worker model when the task can be cleanly split into known subtasks, but monitor the orchestrator for bottlenecks. Reach for the blackboard approach when the problem space is open-ended and the solution path must evolve dynamically, accepting added testing and debugging complexity. Use the pipeline pattern for rigid, repeatable workflows where simplicity and predictability outweigh flexibility. Matching the pattern to the problem’s structure keeps coordination overhead manageable and prevents hidden failure modes from surfacing months after launch.
